title: Data from Configuration Repository: Network Device Configuration Dump
shortTitle: Data from Configuration Repository: Network Device Config...
summary: Network Device Configuration Dump is the sub-technique of Data from Configuration Repository in which the adversary retrieves complete configuration files from network devices rather than walking individual management variables. Device configuration holds the parameters that decide how the device operates: interface addressing, routing and access control rules, logging destinations, device identity for authentication services, and very often reusable secrets such as service account names, encrypted or weakly protected passwords, shared keys and certificate references. Each device normally keeps a working copy in memory and a separate copy on non volatile storage that is loaded after a reset, so an adversary can read either the live running configuration or the saved startup file, or instruct the device to export it for offline review. Retrieval uses ordinary management routes, including management protocols, terminal or console sessions and vendor management applications, all of which are legitimate functions that leave only routine looking records unless the account, source and volume are examined. Detection rests on configuration management and command auditing: full configuration reads or exports by an unexpected account, downloads of many device configurations in a short period, backup jobs running outside their schedule, management sessions from hosts outside the designated management network, and exports written to unusual destinations. Legitimate activity comes from the backup server or automation platform, on a known schedule, with read only credentials.

beginner.definition: Every network device keeps a configuration file. It records addresses, routes, security rules and account details that tell the device how to work. This sub-technique describes an attacker taking copies of those files.
beginner.whyItMatters: Configuration files often contain account names, shared secrets and keys. They also describe how the network is built and where its defences sit. Taking them changes nothing on the device, so normal monitoring sees no attack. With these files an attacker can plan a route through the network and log in as a trusted service.
howItWorks: The attacker first reaches the device through a management session or protocol.
They ask the device to display or export its full running configuration file.
The running configuration is the copy the device is using right now.
They may also read the saved copy that loads after a restart.
They repeat this across many devices and store the collected files together.
The files reveal topology, defences and credentials for many later attack steps.
beginner.example: A hospital keeps a short summary sheet at the night desk, but the full building plans live in a locked drawer. The summary says which rooms exist. The plans show the wiring, the alarms, the staff lockers and where the drug cupboard keys are kept. A thief who photographs the plans learns far more than a thief who only reads the summary. A full configuration dump is those plans. It is not a single detail about one device; it is the complete instruction set showing how the whole building is wired and protected.
takeaways: Configuration files are secrets and should be stored and moved like secrets.
Audit who exports configurations and from where, and alert on new sources.
Encrypt configuration backups and remove plain text shared secrets.

objectives: Describe what a network device configuration file contains and why it is sensitive.
Explain the difference between the running configuration and the saved startup copy.
Identify command and export records that show a configuration was taken.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from reading the Management Information Base.
Compare a scheduled backup job with unauthorised configuration collection.
Describe how stolen configuration data supports later access.
